### Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Compute **Gini impurity** ($1 - \sum p_k^2$), **base-2 Shannon entropy** ($-\sum p_k \log_2 p_k$), and greedy **CART decision stump** midpoint splits from scratch in pure NumPy.
2. Diagnose the **bias–variance trade-off** of single Decision Trees by sweeping `max_depth` and measuring the generalization gap (`train_auc - val_auc`).
3. Contrast **Bagging** (`RandomForestClassifier` with parallel bootstrap trees and **Out-of-Bag (OOB)** validation) against **Gradient Boosting** (`HistGradientBoostingClassifier` fitting sequential residuals, plus its conceptual relationship to **XGBoost** and **LightGBM**).
4. Explain why `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` handles missing (`NaN`) clinical measurements natively while classic `GradientBoostingClassifier` raises `ValueError`.
5. Unmask the high-cardinality bias of default training-set **Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI)** by contrasting `.feature_importances_` against held-out **Permutation Importance** (`sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance`).
6. Implement exact **3-feature Shapley value attribution** across all $3! = 6$ permutations, verify the **Efficiency Axiom** ($\phi_0 + \sum_i \phi_i = f(x)$), and interpret local SHAP explanations for clinical risk prediction.

## Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Trees & Ensembles Rule Tabular Science {#sec-ch24-intuition}

Linear and logistic regression assume that every predictor shifts the log-odds smoothly along a straight line. Real clinical and epidemiological data rarely obey neat straight lines:

- **Threshold Effects:** Maternal hemoglobin below $11.0\text{ g/dL}$ signals clinical anemia, and fewer than $4$ antenatal care (ANC) visits marks WHO-defined inadequate care. A **Decision Tree** discovers these exact cutoffs automatically.
- **Automatic Feature Interactions:** Low wealth paired with fewer than $4$ ANC visits may elevate child stunting risk far beyond the sum of either factor alone. Every root-to-leaf path in a tree is a natural interaction rule (`wealth_rank <= 2.5 AND anc_visits <= 3.5`).
- **Monotonic Scale Invariance:** Because trees split on order thresholds ($x \le t$), you do **not** need `StandardScaler` or log-transforms for tree splits to work.

Yet a single unconstrained Decision Tree has an Achilles' heel: **extreme variance**. Grow a tree deep enough and it creates one tiny leaf per training household—scoring near `1.000` training AUC while collapsing on new patients.

Modern machine learning solves single-tree fragility through two complementary **ensemble** philosophies:

- **Bagging & Random Forests (Variance Reduction in Parallel):** Train $B$ deep trees independently on bootstrap resamples of the training rows, randomly restricting each split to a subset of features (`max_features="sqrt"`). Averaging decorrelated trees slashes variance dramatically, and the ~36.8% of rows omitted from each bootstrap sample provide near-free **Out-of-Bag (OOB)** validation!
- **Gradient Boosting (Bias Reduction in Sequence):** Train shallow trees ("weak learners") one after another, where each new tree predicts the **residual error** left behind by the ensemble so far, scaled by a shrinkage **learning rate** $\eta$.
- **Histogram Boosting, XGBoost & LightGBM:** Modern boosting libraries (`HistGradientBoostingClassifier`, XGBoost, and LightGBM) bin continuous features into ~255 quantile histograms (making split search $10\times$–$100\times$ faster), apply $L_2$ leaf regularization, and learn optimal split directions for missing (`NaN`) values natively.

| Framework | Tree Growth | Native `NaN`? | Core Strengths in Research |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **Scikit-Learn `HistGradientBoosting`** | Leaf-wise (binned) | Yes | Zero extra installs; native `Pipeline` fit |
| **XGBoost (`xgboost`)** | Depth-wise (exact/hist) | Yes | $L_1$/$L_2$ leaf penalties; GPU & sparse data |
| **LightGBM (`lightgbm`)** | Leaf-wise (GOSS/EFB) | Yes | Fastest on $100\text{k}+$ rows; native categories |

: Conceptual comparison of modern Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) engines.

Finally, predictive accuracy alone never earns clinical trust. Peer reviewers demand **interpretability**—both **global** (which predictors drive discrimination on held-out patients?) and **local** (why did the model assign *this specific household* a 25.7% stunting probability?). Held-out **Permutation Importance** answers the global question without MDI's high-cardinality trap, while **Shapley values (SHAP)** answer the local question with game-theoretic fairness.

::: {.callout-note title="Mental Model — Two Axes of Tree Interpretability"}
Always separate **global** from **local** explanations in your methods section:

1. **Global (Held-Out Permutation Importance):** Shuffle one feature column at a time on the **test set** and measure how much ROC-AUC drops. Noise features collapse near zero.
2. **Local (Shapley / SHAP Values):** Explain one patient's prediction $f(x)$ as a baseline risk $\phi_0$ plus additive feature credits $\phi_1 + \phi_2 + \dots + \phi_p = f(x) - \phi_0$, averaged across every possible ordering of features.
:::

## Stage 2 — Visual Mental Model: Bagging vs. Boosting & Interpretability {#sec-ch24-mental-model}

Compare how **Bagging (Random Forests)** averages independent parallel trees to cut variance, while **Boosting (`HistGradientBoosting`)** chains shallow residual trees sequentially to cut bias—and how both feed into held-out interpretability:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 5.6
%%| fig-align: center
flowchart TD
    subgraph Data["Training Cohort"]
        D0["Clean Features X, Target y<br/>(Stratified 75/25 Split)"]
    end
    subgraph Bag["Bagging: Parallel"]
        B1["Bootstrap 1 -> Tree 1<br/>(max_features=sqrt)"]
        B2["Bootstrap 2 -> Tree 2<br/>(OOB Rows Held Out)"]
        B3["Average Probabilities<br/>Low Variance + OOB Score"]
    end
    subgraph Boost["Boosting: Serial"]
        G1["Init F0 -> Shallow Tree 1<br/>Fits Residuals r1 = y - F0"]
        G2["Update F1 = F0 + lr * T1<br/>Tree 2 Fits Residuals r2"]
        G3["Additive Ensemble F_M<br/>Low Bias + Native NaNs"]
    end
    subgraph Explain["Interpretability"]
        E1["Global: Permutation AUC<br/>(Held-Out Test Set)"]
        E2["Local: Shapley Values<br/>phi_0 + sum(phi_i) = f(x)"]
    end
    D0 --> B1
    D0 --> B2
    B1 --> B3
    B2 --> B3
    D0 --> G1
    G1 --> G2
    G2 --> G3
    B3 --> E1
    G3 --> E1
    E1 --> E2
```

Notice the structural contrast at a glance: in **Bagging**, Tree 1 and Tree 2 never communicate—they train in parallel on different bootstrap draws so their errors cancel when averaged. In **Boosting**, Tree 2 *cannot begin* until Tree 1 finishes and exposes the remaining residuals $r_1$.

::: {.callout-warning title="Three Silent Tree & Ensemble Pitfalls in Real Studies"}
1. **Default `.feature_importances_` (MDI) Favors Noise:** Impurity-based importance is computed on the *training* set and systematically inflates high-cardinality continuous features—even pure random IDs! Always audit with held-out `permutation_importance`.
2. **Unbounded Depth Memorizes Small Cohorts:** A single tree with `max_depth=None` can hit `train_auc = 1.000` while dropping below a simple stump on validation. Always inspect `train_auc - val_auc`.
3. **Never Assume Boosting Automatically Wins on Small $n$:** On a $500$-row public-health survey, shallow regularized trees or logistic models can rival or beat un-tuned ensembles. Always benchmark all three families empirically on the same stratified split!
:::

### Setup: Loading & Preparing `mch_survey_sample` {#sec-ch24-setup}

```python
import itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    GradientBoostingClassifier,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    RandomForestClassifier,
)
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor
import sharukh_tutor as tutor

mch_raw = tutor.load_data("mch_survey_sample", as_pandas=True)
mch = mch_raw.copy()
mch["residence"] = mch["residence"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
mch["anc_visits"] = mch["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
mch["is_urban"] = (mch["residence"] == "Urban").astype(int)
wealth_map = {
    "Poorest": 1, "Poorer": 2, "Middle": 3, "Richer": 4, "Richest": 5
}
mch["wealth_rank"] = mch["wealth_quintile"].map(wealth_map)

features = [
    "maternal_age_years", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl",
    "is_urban", "wealth_rank",
]
clean = mch[features + ["child_stunted"]].dropna()
X = clean[features]
y = clean["child_stunted"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=42
)
print("Clean complete-case shape:", clean.shape)
print(f"Train: {len(X_train)}, Test: {len(X_test)}, "
      f"Stunting rate: {y.mean():.4f}")
```

**Expected Output:**
```text
Clean complete-case shape: (470, 6)
Train: 352, Test: 118, Stunting rate: 0.1383
```

Notice two crucial data-hygiene steps before fitting any tree:

- **Sentinel replacement (`999 -> np.nan`):** If `999` stayed inside `anc_visits`, a tree would treat missingness as "999 clinic visits"—an extreme right-tail artifact.
- **Ordinal mapping (`wealth_rank` 1..5):** Mapping `"Poorest"` through `"Richest"` to integers `1..5` preserves the socioeconomic ordering so a single split (`wealth_rank <= 2.5`) separates the bottom two quintiles from the upper three cleanly.
- **Stratified split (`stratify=y`):** Because child stunting prevalence is imbalanced (`13.83%`), stratifying preserves the exact same class ratio in both train (`352` rows) and test (`118` rows).

### Gini Impurity, Shannon Entropy & Greedy Decision Stump {#sec-ch24-impurity}

For a node with class proportions $p_1, \dots, p_K$, CART measures node disorder using **Gini impurity** or **base-2 Shannon entropy**:

$$G(y) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k^2, \qquad H(y) = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k \log_2(p_k)$$

A **decision stump** tests every midpoint $t$ between consecutive sorted unique values of feature $x$ and picks the threshold minimizing weighted child Gini:

$$G_{\text{split}}(t) = \frac{n_L}{n} G(y_{x \le t}) + \frac{n_R}{n} G(y_{x > t})$$

```python
def gini_demo(y_vals):
    arr = np.asarray(y_vals)
    if arr.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / arr.size
    return round(float(1.0 - np.sum(probs ** 2)), 4)

def entropy_demo(y_vals):
    arr = np.asarray(y_vals)
    if arr.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / arr.size
    return round(float(-np.sum(probs * np.log2(probs))), 4)

def stump_demo(x_vals, y_vals):
    x = np.asarray(x_vals, dtype=float)
    yv = np.asarray(y_vals)
    uniq = np.unique(x)
    mids = (uniq[:-1] + uniq[1:]) / 2.0
    best_t, best_g = float(mids[0]), float("inf")
    for t in mids:
        left, right = yv[x <= t], yv[x > t]
        wg = (len(left) / len(yv)) * gini_demo(left)
        wg += (len(right) / len(yv)) * gini_demo(right)
        if wg < best_g:
            best_g, best_t = wg, float(t)
    return (round(best_t, 4), round(best_g, 4))

print("Root Gini:", gini_demo(y_train),
      "| Root Entropy:", entropy_demo(y_train))
for col in ["wealth_rank", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl"]:
    t, g = stump_demo(X_train[col], y_train)
    print(f"Best stump on {col:16s}: thresh={t:.2f}, w_gini={g:.4f}")
```

**Expected Output:**
```text
Root Gini: 0.2397 | Root Entropy: 0.5822
Best stump on wealth_rank     : thresh=2.50, w_gini=0.2171
Best stump on anc_visits      : thresh=3.50, w_gini=0.2259
Best stump on maternal_hb_g_dl: thresh=15.10, w_gini=0.2354
```

Look at the epidemiology our pure-NumPy stump just discovered automatically:

- **`wealth_rank <= 2.50` (`w_gini = 0.2171`):** Achieves the largest impurity drop (`0.2397 -> 0.2171`) by separating `Poorest`/`Poorer` households from `Middle`/`Richer`/`Richest`.
- **`anc_visits <= 3.50` (`w_gini = 0.2259`):** Rediscovers the World Health Organization's classic **4+ antenatal care visits** benchmark (`<= 3` vs. `>= 4`) directly from data!

### Decision Tree Overfitting & Depth Sweep {#sec-ch24-depth}

```python
depth_rows = []
for d in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12]:
    dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=42)
    dt.fit(X_train, y_train)
    tr_auc = roc_auc_score(y_train, dt.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1])
    te_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, dt.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
    depth_rows.append({
        "max_depth": d,
        "train_auc": round(float(tr_auc), 4),
        "val_auc": round(float(te_auc), 4),
        "gap": round(float(tr_auc - te_auc), 4),
    })
print(pd.DataFrame(depth_rows).to_string(index=False))
```

**Expected Output:**
```text
 max_depth  train_auc  val_auc    gap
         1     0.7200   0.6213 0.0987
         2     0.7544   0.6152 0.1392
         3     0.7964   0.6400 0.1564
         5     0.8854   0.6550 0.2304
         8     0.9465   0.6354 0.3111
        12     0.9993   0.5809 0.4184
```

This table is the textbook signature of **tree overfitting**:

- From `max_depth = 1` to `5`, validation ROC-AUC climbs from `0.6213` to **`0.6550`**.
- Beyond depth `5`, training AUC shoots to **`0.9993`** (nearly memorizing every single household!), while validation AUC plunges to **`0.5809`**—a massive generalization gap of **`0.4184`**!

### Bagging, Random Forests & Out-of-Bag (OOB) Validation {#sec-ch24-oob}

When a Random Forest draws a bootstrap sample of size $n$ with replacement, the probability that any given household is *never* selected in a single tree is $(1 - 1/n)^n \approx e^{-1} \approx \mathbf{0.368}$. Evaluating every household using only the ~36.8% of trees that never saw it produces the **Out-of-Bag (OOB) score**—free internal validation without touching the test set!

```python
oob_rows = []
for d in [2, 4, 6, 8, 12]:
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=120, max_depth=d, oob_score=True, random_state=42
    ).fit(X_train, y_train)
    oob_rows.append({
        "max_depth": d,
        "oob_score": round(float(rf.oob_score_), 4),
    })
print(pd.DataFrame(oob_rows).to_string(index=False))
```

**Expected Output:**
```text
 max_depth  oob_score
         2     0.8608
         4     0.8636
         6     0.8580
         8     0.8466
        12     0.8494
```

OOB validation cleanly peaks at **`max_depth = 4` (`0.8636`)** and declines as deeper trees memorize noise in the bootstrap draws. Remember: `oob_score_` reports accuracy by default, so always confirm discrimination on imbalanced outcomes with ROC-AUC and PR-AUC.

### Gradient Boosting Residuals, Native `NaN`s & Ensemble Scaling {#sec-ch24-boost}

In Gradient Boosting, each tree $h_m(x)$ fits the **pseudo-residuals** left over by the previous ensemble $F_{m-1}(x)$ and updates predictions cautiously via learning rate $\eta$:

$$r_i^{(m)} = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i), \qquad F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \eta \cdot h_m(x)$$

```python
# 1. Sequential residual fitting intuition (3 boosting rounds)
y_hb = np.array([9.4, 10.1, 11.2, 12.6, 13.0])
x_anc = np.array([[0], [1], [3], [6], [8]])
pred = np.full_like(y_hb, y_hb.mean())
lr = 0.5
print(f"Step 0 (mean)   MSE: {np.mean((y_hb - pred) ** 2):.4f}")
for step in range(1, 4):
    resid = y_hb - pred
    stump = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1, random_state=42)
    stump.fit(x_anc, resid)
    pred = pred + lr * stump.predict(x_anc)
    print(f"Step {step} (boost) MSE: {np.mean((y_hb - pred) ** 2):.4f}")

# 2. Native NaN handling of HistGradientBoosting on all 500 MCH rows
X_full = mch[features]
y_full = mch["child_stunted"]
Xf_tr, Xf_te, yf_tr, yf_te = train_test_split(
    X_full, y_full, test_size=0.25, stratify=y_full, random_state=42
)
hgb_nan = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=42)
hgb_nan.fit(Xf_tr, yf_tr)
nan_auc = roc_auc_score(yf_te, hgb_nan.predict_proba(Xf_te)[:, 1])
n_nans = int(X_full.isna().sum().sum())
print(f"HGB native NaN (n={len(X_full)}, NaNs={n_nans}) "
      f"test ROC-AUC: {nan_auc:.4f}")

# 3. Ensemble scaling on a 600-row nonlinear cohort
X_syn, y_syn = make_classification(
    n_samples=600, n_features=6, n_informative=4, n_redundant=1,
    weights=[0.80, 0.20], random_state=42,
)
Xs_tr, Xs_te, ys_tr, ys_te = train_test_split(
    X_syn, y_syn, test_size=0.25, stratify=y_syn, random_state=42
)
specs = [
    ("DecisionTree", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=42)),
    ("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=42)),
    ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
        max_depth=4, random_state=42)),
]
for name, clf in specs:
    clf.fit(Xs_tr, ys_tr)
    p = clf.predict_proba(Xs_te)[:, 1]
    print(f"Synth {name:20s} ROC={roc_auc_score(ys_te, p):.4f} "
          f"PR={average_precision_score(ys_te, p):.4f}")
```

**Expected Output:**
```text
Step 0 (mean)   MSE: 1.9264
Step 1 (boost) MSE: 0.7406
Step 2 (boost) MSE: 0.2439
Step 3 (boost) MSE: 0.1090
HGB native NaN (n=500, NaNs=30) test ROC-AUC: 0.7004
Synth DecisionTree         ROC=0.8162 PR=0.6082
Synth RandomForest         ROC=0.8932 PR=0.7627
Synth HistGradientBoosting ROC=0.9246 PR=0.8237
```

Three powerful lessons jump out of this output:

1. **Residual Shrinkage in Action:** Just three depth-1 stumps shrink MSE from `1.9264` down to `0.1090` by focusing every new stump strictly on the unexplained error of earlier rounds.
2. **Native Missing-Value Splitting Wins:** Instead of dropping 30 households with missing hemoglobin or ANC values, `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` trains directly on all **500** rows with `30` `NaN`s intact and leaps to **`ROC-AUC = 0.7004`**!
3. **Ensemble Dominance on Nonlinear Tabular Signal:** On the 600-row nonlinear cohort, `HistGradientBoosting` (`ROC = 0.9246, PR = 0.8237`) decisively beats `RandomForest` (`0.8932 / 0.7627`), which in turn crushes a single `DecisionTree` (`0.8162 / 0.6082`).

### Interpretability: Permutation Importance vs. Default MDI Bias {#sec-ch24-perm}

Let's test Scikit-Learn's default `.feature_importances_` (Mean Decrease in Impurity, MDI) by injecting a **pure random noise column** (`random_noise_id`) into `mch_survey_sample`:

```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
noisy = clean.copy()
noisy["random_noise_id"] = rng.uniform(0, 1000, size=len(noisy))
f_noise = features + ["random_noise_id"]
Xn_tr, Xn_te, yn_tr, yn_te = train_test_split(
    noisy[f_noise], noisy["child_stunted"],
    test_size=0.25, stratify=noisy["child_stunted"], random_state=42,
)
rf_noise = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=42
).fit(Xn_tr, yn_tr)
pi_noise = permutation_importance(
    rf_noise, Xn_te, yn_te, scoring="roc_auc",
    n_repeats=10, random_state=42,
)
imp_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "feature": f_noise,
    "mdi_impurity": np.round(rf_noise.feature_importances_, 4),
    "perm_auc_mean": np.round(pi_noise.importances_mean, 4),
    "perm_auc_std": np.round(pi_noise.importances_std, 4),
}).sort_values("mdi_impurity", ascending=False)
print(imp_df.to_string(index=False))
```

**Expected Output:**
```text
           feature  mdi_impurity  perm_auc_mean  perm_auc_std
   random_noise_id        0.2316         0.0140        0.0185
  maternal_hb_g_dl        0.2307         0.0081        0.0229
        anc_visits        0.1795         0.0275        0.0489
       wealth_rank        0.1719         0.1135        0.0626
maternal_age_years        0.1500        -0.0129        0.0159
          is_urban        0.0362         0.0069        0.0113
```

Pause and absorb how staggering that table is:

- **Default MDI (`mdi_impurity`) ranked pure random noise #1 (`0.2316`)**—above genuine socioeconomic driver `wealth_rank` (`0.1719`)! Why? Because a continuous uniform column has 352 unique split candidates to slice training noise, whereas `wealth_rank` only has 4 possible split points (`1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5`).
- **Held-Out Permutation Importance (`perm_auc_mean`) immediately unmasks the fraud:** Shuffling `wealth_rank` on the test set slashes ROC-AUC by **`+0.1135`**, ranking it #1 by a landslide, while `random_noise_id` collapses to `0.0140 ± 0.0185` (indistinguishable from zero!).

### Exact 3-Feature Shapley Values (SHAP Intuition) From Scratch {#sec-ch24-shap}

How do we explain **one individual household's** predicted stunting probability $f(x)$? Cooperative game theory's **Shapley value** treats each feature as a player joining a coalition from a reference `baseline_row` to `x_row`. Because tree models contain feature interactions, the marginal credit of revealing feature $i$ depends on *which features were already revealed*. Averaging across all $p!$ permutations yields the unique attribution satisfying **Efficiency**, **Symmetry**, **Dummy**, and **Additivity**:

$$\phi_i(x) = \frac{1}{p!} \sum_{\pi \in S_p} \Big[ f\big(S_\pi(i) \cup \{i\}\big) - f\big(S_\pi(i)\big) \Big], \qquad \phi_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i(x) = f(x)$$

```python
top3 = ["wealth_rank", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl"]
rf3 = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=100, max_depth=4, random_state=42
).fit(X_train[top3].to_numpy(), y_train.to_numpy())

def rf3_proba(v):
    arr = np.asarray(v, dtype=float).reshape(1, -1)
    return float(rf3.predict_proba(arr)[0, 1])

def shapley_3_demo(predict_fn, x_row, base_row):
    x = np.asarray(x_row, dtype=float)
    base = np.asarray(base_row, dtype=float)
    base_val = float(predict_fn(base))
    pred_val = float(predict_fn(x))
    contribs = np.zeros(3, dtype=float)
    perms = list(itertools.permutations([0, 1, 2]))
    for perm in perms:
        state = base.copy()
        prev = base_val
        for idx in perm:
            state[idx] = x[idx]
            curr = float(predict_fn(state))
            contribs[idx] += curr - prev
            prev = curr
    shap_vals = contribs / len(perms)
    return {
        "base_value": round(base_val, 4),
        "shap_values": [round(float(v), 4) for v in shap_vals],
        "prediction": round(pred_val, 4),
    }

baseline = X_train[top3].median().to_numpy()
high_risk = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 9.5])
sh = shapley_3_demo(rf3_proba, high_risk, baseline)
print("Baseline (median):", np.round(baseline, 2).tolist())
print("High-risk patient:", high_risk.tolist())
print("Base:", sh["base_value"], "| Pred:", sh["prediction"])
print("Shapley values:", sh["shap_values"])
eff = round(sh["base_value"] + sum(sh["shap_values"]), 4)
print(f"Efficiency check: {eff} ~= {sh['prediction']}")
```

**Expected Output:**
```text
Baseline (median): [3.0, 4.0, 11.5]
High-risk patient: [1.0, 1.0, 9.5]
Base: 0.0365 | Pred: 0.257
Shapley values: [0.1839, 0.0408, -0.0043]
Efficiency check: 0.2569 ~= 0.257
```

Read this patient-level waterfall attribution like a clinician:

- Starting from the median household baseline (`wealth_rank = 3`, `anc_visits = 4`, `Hb = 11.5 g/dL`), predicted stunting risk is **`3.65%`** (`base_value = 0.0365`).
- For a household in the poorest quintile (`wealth_rank = 1`) with only `1` ANC visit and `Hb = 9.5 g/dL`, risk jumps to **`25.70%`** (`prediction = 0.2570`).
- Exact Shapley values decompose that `+22.05` percentage-point surge cleanly: **`+18.39 pp`** from `wealth_rank`, **`+4.08 pp`** from low `anc_visits`, and **`-0.43 pp`** from `maternal_hb_g_dl`.
- **Production Bridge (`shap` Library):** For $p = 3$ features, $3! = 6$ permutations is instant; for $p = 30$ features, $30! \approx 2.65 \times 10^{32}$ is impossible by brute force! In full research pipelines, the `shap` library's **TreeSHAP** (`shap.TreeExplainer(model)`) exploits tree path structure to compute these exact same Shapley values in polynomial time $O(T L D^2)$.

### Break It On Purpose! (Tree & Ensemble Error Anatomy) {#sec-ch24-errors}

::: {.callout-important title="Break It On Purpose #1 — ValueError / InvalidParameterError (`max_depth=0`)"}
```python
bad_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=0, random_state=42)
bad_tree.fit(X_train, y_train)
```
**Python's Traceback:**
```text
InvalidParameterError: The 'max_depth' parameter of DecisionTreeClassifier
must be an int in the range [1, inf) or None. Got 0 instead.
```
**Diagnosis:** `InvalidParameterError` (a subclass of `ValueError`) fires because a decision tree must have at least depth `1` (a decision stump) or `None` (grow until leaves are pure). Setting `max_depth=0` leaves zero splits possible.  
**Fix:** Use `max_depth >= 1` (e.g., `1` for a stump, `3..6` for regularized trees) or `max_depth=None` when intentionally testing an unpruned tree.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Break It On Purpose #2 — ValueError (`oob_score=True` With `bootstrap=False`)"}
```python
bad_rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=50, oob_score=True, bootstrap=False, random_state=42
)
bad_rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
```
**Python's Traceback:**
```text
ValueError: Out of bag estimation only available if bootstrap=True
```
**Diagnosis:** Out-of-Bag scoring depends mathematically on bootstrap resampling with replacement leaving ~36.8% of training rows unused in each tree. When `bootstrap=False`, every tree sees 100% of rows, so no out-of-bag rows exist!  
**Fix:** Keep the default `bootstrap=True` whenever `oob_score=True`, or use $k$-fold cross-validation if you deliberately disable bootstrapping.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Break It On Purpose #3 — ValueError (Passing `NaN`s Into Classic `GradientBoostingClassifier`)"}
```python
bad_gbc = GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42)
bad_gbc.fit(Xf_tr, yf_tr)
```
**Python's Traceback:**
```text
ValueError: Input X contains NaN.
GradientBoostingClassifier does not accept missing values encoded as NaN
natively. For supervised learning, you might want to consider
sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier and Regressor which
accept missing values encoded as NaNs natively.
```
**Diagnosis:** Classic `GradientBoostingClassifier` (like `LogisticRegression` and pre-1.4 versions of `RandomForestClassifier`) refuses `NaN` inputs and crashes during `.fit()`.  
**Fix:** Either wrap the estimator in a leakage-free `Pipeline([("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("clf", ...)])`, drop incomplete rows intentionally, or switch directly to `HistGradientBoostingClassifier`, which learns optimal left/right branches for missing values natively.
:::

## Stage 4 — The Researcher's Problem-Structuring Blueprint {#sec-ch24-blueprint}

**Scenario:** Your maternal-and-child health research team needs a single reproducible benchmark function `run_stunting_tree_audit(raw_df, seed=42)` that takes raw `mch_survey_sample` (without mutating it), cleans all survey artifacts, compares Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Histogram Gradient Boosting on a stratified 75/25 split using both ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, and identifies the top held-out risk driver via permutation importance on the winning model.

### Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

1. **Hygiene & Feature Engineering (Zero Mutation):**

   - Copy `raw_df` first (`work = raw_df.copy()`).
   - Standardize `residence` casing, replace `anc_visits == 999` with `np.nan`, derive binary `is_urban`, map ordinal `wealth_quintile` (`Poorest: 1 .. Richest: 5`) to `wealth_rank`, and drop incomplete rows across the 5 features + `child_stunted`.

2. **Stratified Multi-Family Benchmark:**

   - Split 75/25 stratified on `child_stunted` with `random_state=seed`.
   - Fit `DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5)`, `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=6)`, and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_depth=4)`, scoring test probabilities (`[:, 1]`) with `roc_auc_score` and `average_precision_score`.
   - Sort the leaderboard descending by `roc_auc`.

3. **Held-Out Interpretability Audit & Verification:**

   - Run `permutation_importance` (`scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=10`) on the **winning** fitted model using `(X_test, y_test)` to extract `top_feature`.
   - Verify complete-case size (`n = 470`), confirm the winning model empirically rather than assuming boosting always wins on small $n$, and check that `wealth_rank` emerges as the top held-out driver.

### Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in `01_walkthrough.ipynb`)

```python
def run_stunting_tree_audit(raw_df, seed=42):
    """Clean MCH data, benchmark 3 tree models, and audit top driver."""
    work = raw_df.copy()
    work["residence"] = (
        work["residence"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
    )
    work["anc_visits"] = work["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
    work["is_urban"] = (work["residence"] == "Urban").astype(int)
    w_map = {
        "Poorest": 1, "Poorer": 2, "Middle": 3,
        "Richer": 4, "Richest": 5,
    }
    work["wealth_rank"] = (
        work["wealth_quintile"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
        .map(w_map)
    )
    feats = [
        "maternal_age_years", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl",
        "is_urban", "wealth_rank",
    ]
    df = work[feats + ["child_stunted"]].dropna()
    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
        df[feats], df["child_stunted"].astype(int),
        test_size=0.25, stratify=df["child_stunted"], random_state=seed,
    )
    models = [
        ("DecisionTree", DecisionTreeClassifier(
            max_depth=5, random_state=seed)),
        ("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=seed)),
        ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
            max_depth=4, random_state=seed)),
    ]
    rows, fitted = [], {}
    for name, clf in models:
        clf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
        proba = clf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
        rows.append({
            "model": name,
            "roc_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_te, proba)), 4),
            "pr_auc": round(
                float(average_precision_score(y_te, proba)), 4
            ),
        })
        fitted[name] = clf
    board = (
        pd.DataFrame(rows)
        .sort_values("roc_auc", ascending=False)
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )
    winner = str(board.iloc[0]["model"])
    pi = permutation_importance(
        fitted[winner], X_te, y_te, scoring="roc_auc",
        n_repeats=10, random_state=seed,
    )
    top_feat = feats[int(np.argmax(pi.importances_mean))]
    return board, winner, top_feat

board, winner, top_feat = run_stunting_tree_audit(mch_raw, seed=42)
print(board.to_string(index=False))
print(f"Winning model: {winner} | Top held-out driver: {top_feat}")
```

**Output:**
```text
               model  roc_auc  pr_auc
        DecisionTree   0.6550  0.2242
HistGradientBoosting   0.6029  0.1897
        RandomForest   0.5827  0.1776
Winning model: DecisionTree | Top held-out driver: wealth_rank
```

Notice the authentic scientific takeaway: on a small complete-case survey ($n = 470$, $118$ test households), a regularized shallow `DecisionTree(max_depth=5)` actually outperforms default ensembles on this split—reminding us why **No Free Lunch** holds and why every manuscript must benchmark simple baselines fairly!

## Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem {#sec-ch24-solutions}

### A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

1. **Gini:** $1 - (0.75^2 + 0.25^2) = 1 - (0.5625 + 0.0625) = \mathbf{0.375}$. **Entropy:** **Less than `1.0` bit** (specifically `0.8113` bits), because binary Shannon entropy achieves its maximum of `1.0` bit only at a 50/50 split.
2. Midpoints are `(2.0 + 4.0) / 2 = 3.0` and `(4.0 + 10.0) / 2 = 7.0`. Threshold **`t = 3.0`** places `[1]` on the left (pure, Gini = `0.0`) and `[0, 0]` on the right (pure, Gini = `0.0`), giving weighted Gini **`0.0`**.
3. **High variance (overfitting):** The depth-12 tree has near-zero training error (`0.9993`) because it memorized idiosyncratic training noise, causing test AUC to collapse (`0.5809`).
4. Approximately **`36.8%`** ($1/e$) of training rows are Out-of-Bag for any single bootstrap tree. Setting `bootstrap=False` trains every tree on 100% of training rows, leaving zero OOB rows to evaluate and triggering `ValueError`.
5. **`max_features="sqrt"`** produces much better decorrelation! With `max_features=None`, nearly every tree splits on `wealth_rank` at the root, yielding highly correlated trees whose average barely reduces variance.
6. **`RandomForestClassifier`: Yes**, all 100 bootstrap trees are completely independent and train in parallel (`n_jobs=-1`). **`HistGradientBoostingClassifier`: No across trees**, because tree $m$ depends sequentially on the residuals of tree $m - 1$ (parallelism happens *within* each tree's histogram bin search instead).
7. You must **increase `max_iter`** (train more boosting rounds), because each smaller step $\eta = 0.01$ corrects only 1% of the residual per tree.
8. Default MDI sums training-set impurity reductions across splits; a unique 10-digit ID offers $n - 1$ split thresholds to memorize training labels. Held-out **`sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance`** on `(X_test, y_test)` exposes the ID immediately by showing near-zero (or negative) test-AUC drop.
9. $\phi_0 = f(0, 0) = \mathbf{1.0}$ and $f(1, 1) = 1 + 2 + 4 = \mathbf{7.0}$.
   - Order `(0, 1)`: reveal $x_1$: $f(1, 0) - f(0, 0) = 3 - 1 = +2$; reveal $x_2$: $f(1, 1) - f(1, 0) = 7 - 3 = +4$.
   - Order `(1, 0)`: reveal $x_2$: $f(0, 1) - f(0, 0) = 1 - 1 = 0$; reveal $x_1$: $f(1, 1) - f(0, 1) = 7 - 1 = +6$.
   - Averaging both orders: $\phi_1 = (2 + 6)/2 = \mathbf{4.0}$, $\phi_2 = (4 + 0)/2 = \mathbf{2.0}$. Efficiency check: $1.0 + 4.0 + 2.0 = \mathbf{7.0} = f(1, 1)$!
10. (a) Switch to **`HistGradientBoostingClassifier`**, which learns optimal missing-value branch routing natively; or (b) wrap `GradientBoostingClassifier` inside a **`Pipeline`** preceded by `SimpleImputer(strategy="median")` fit strictly on `X_train`.

### B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in `02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb`)

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    RandomForestClassifier,
)
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# To-Do 24.1
def gini_impurity(y):
    """Compute Gini impurity 1 - sum(p_k^2) rounded to 4 decimals."""
    arr = np.asarray(y)
    if arr.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / arr.size
    return round(float(1.0 - np.sum(probs ** 2)), 4)

# To-Do 24.2
def shannon_entropy(y):
    """Compute base-2 Shannon entropy rounded to 4 decimals."""
    arr = np.asarray(y)
    if arr.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / arr.size
    probs = probs[probs > 0]
    ent = float(-np.sum(probs * np.log2(probs)))
    return round(0.0 if ent == 0.0 else ent, 4)

# To-Do 24.3
def best_stump_split(x_feature, y):
    """Find midpoint threshold minimizing weighted Gini impurity."""
    def _gini(arr):
        if arr.size == 0:
            return 0.0
        _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
        probs = counts / arr.size
        return float(1.0 - np.sum(probs ** 2))

    x = np.asarray(x_feature, dtype=float)
    y_arr = np.asarray(y)
    uniq = np.unique(x)
    mids = (uniq[:-1] + uniq[1:]) / 2.0
    best_t, best_g = float(mids[0]), float("inf")
    n = y_arr.size
    for t in mids:
        left = y_arr[x <= t]
        right = y_arr[x > t]
        wg = (left.size / n) * _gini(left) + (right.size / n) * _gini(right)
        if wg < best_g:
            best_g = wg
            best_t = float(t)
    return (round(best_t, 4), round(best_g, 4))

# To-Do 24.4
def compare_tree_depths(X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, depths, seed=42):
    """Compare DecisionTree train/val ROC-AUC and gap across depths."""
    rows = []
    for d in depths:
        clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=seed)
        clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
        tr = float(roc_auc_score(y_train, clf.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]))
        va = float(roc_auc_score(y_val, clf.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]))
        rows.append({
            "max_depth": d,
            "train_auc": round(tr, 4),
            "val_auc": round(va, 4),
            "gap": round(tr - va, 4),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

# To-Do 24.5
def fit_ensemble_comparison(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, seed=42):
    """Fit DecisionTree, RandomForest, and HistGradientBoosting."""
    models = [
        ("DecisionTree", DecisionTreeClassifier(
            max_depth=5, random_state=seed)),
        ("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=seed)),
        ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
            max_depth=4, random_state=seed)),
    ]
    rows = []
    for name, clf in models:
        clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
        proba = clf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
        rows.append({
            "model": name,
            "roc_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba)), 4),
            "pr_auc": round(
                float(average_precision_score(y_test, proba)), 4
            ),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

# To-Do 24.6
def compute_permutation_ranking(
    model, X_test, y_test, feature_names, seed=42
):
    """Rank features by held-out ROC-AUC permutation importance."""
    res = permutation_importance(
        model, X_test, y_test, scoring="roc_auc",
        n_repeats=10, random_state=seed,
    )
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "feature": list(feature_names),
        "importance_mean": np.round(res.importances_mean, 4),
        "importance_std": np.round(res.importances_std, 4),
    })
    return df.sort_values(
        "importance_mean", ascending=False
    ).reset_index(drop=True)
```

### C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 24 Coding Exam (Mirrored in `03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb`)

```python
import itertools
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Exam Task 24.1 (30 pts)
def exact_shapley_3features(predict_fn, x_row, baseline_row):
    """Compute exact 3-feature Shapley values over all 6 permutations."""
    x = np.asarray(x_row, dtype=float)
    base = np.asarray(baseline_row, dtype=float)
    base_val = float(predict_fn(base))
    pred_val = float(predict_fn(x))
    contribs = np.zeros(3, dtype=float)
    perms = list(itertools.permutations([0, 1, 2]))
    for perm in perms:
        state = base.copy()
        prev = base_val
        for idx in perm:
            state[idx] = x[idx]
            curr = float(predict_fn(state))
            contribs[idx] += curr - prev
            prev = curr
    shap_vals = contribs / len(perms)
    return {
        "base_value": round(base_val, 4),
        "shap_values": [round(float(v), 4) for v in shap_vals],
        "prediction": round(pred_val, 4),
    }

# Exam Task 24.2 (35 pts)
def tune_random_forest_oob(X_train, y_train, max_depths, seed=42):
    """Select best RandomForest max_depth using Out-of-Bag accuracy."""
    rows = []
    best_depth = int(max_depths[0])
    best_oob = -1.0
    for d in max_depths:
        rf = RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=120, max_depth=d,
            oob_score=True, random_state=seed,
        ).fit(X_train, y_train)
        score = float(rf.oob_score_)
        rows.append({"max_depth": int(d), "oob_score": round(score, 4)})
        if score > best_oob:
            best_oob = score
            best_depth = int(d)
    return {
        "best_depth": best_depth,
        "best_oob_score": round(best_oob, 4),
        "oob_table": pd.DataFrame(rows),
    }

# Exam Task 24.3 (35 pts)
def public_health_tree_benchmark(mch_df, seed=42):
    """Benchmark 3 tree families on MCH stunting and rank top driver."""
    work = mch_df.copy()
    work["residence"] = (
        work["residence"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
    )
    work["anc_visits"] = work["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
    work["is_urban"] = (work["residence"] == "Urban").astype(int)
    w_map = {
        "Poorest": 1, "Poorer": 2, "Middle": 3,
        "Richer": 4, "Richest": 5,
    }
    work["wealth_rank"] = (
        work["wealth_quintile"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
        .map(w_map)
    )
    feats = [
        "maternal_age_years", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl",
        "is_urban", "wealth_rank",
    ]
    clean = work[feats + ["child_stunted"]].dropna()
    X = clean[feats]
    y = clean["child_stunted"].astype(int)
    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=seed
    )
    specs = [
        ("DecisionTree", DecisionTreeClassifier(
            max_depth=5, random_state=seed)),
        ("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=seed)),
        ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
            max_depth=4, random_state=seed)),
    ]
    rows, fitted = [], {}
    for name, clf in specs:
        clf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
        proba = clf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
        rows.append({
            "model": name,
            "roc_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_te, proba)), 4),
            "pr_auc": round(
                float(average_precision_score(y_te, proba)), 4
            ),
        })
        fitted[name] = clf
    leaderboard = (
        pd.DataFrame(rows)
        .sort_values("roc_auc", ascending=False)
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )
    best_model = str(leaderboard.iloc[0]["model"])
    pi = permutation_importance(
        fitted[best_model], X_te, y_te, scoring="roc_auc",
        n_repeats=10, random_state=seed,
    )
    top_feature = feats[int(np.argmax(pi.importances_mean))]
    return {
        "leaderboard": leaderboard,
        "best_model": best_model,
        "top_feature": top_feature,
    }
```

### D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 24 Failure Modes

1. **Passing Hard Class Predictions (`.predict`) Instead of Probabilities (`.predict_proba[:, 1]`) Into ROC-AUC / PR-AUC:** Hard binary labels collapse all probability thresholds to a single operating point, distorting both `roc_auc_score` and `average_precision_score`. Always slice column `1` of `.predict_proba(X)`.
2. **Trusting Default MDI `.feature_importances_` on Mixed-Cardinality Clinical Data:** Training-set impurity gain rewards continuous or ID-like columns with many split thresholds—even pure noise! Always validate global driver rankings with held-out `permutation_importance` on `(X_test, y_test)`.
3. **Evaluating Only One Feature Order When Explaining Nonlinear Models:** In models with feature interactions, changing which feature is turned on first shifts marginal credit dramatically. Averaging across permutations (exact Shapley / TreeSHAP) is the only way to preserve fair attribution and guarantee the Efficiency Axiom $\phi_0 + \sum_i \phi_i = f(x)$.
